corrections.comment: The LLM applies a rule the judge context doesn’t contain (“confident” requires multiple independent sources). pe_004 is backed by the 1850 census with an exact age progression, the same household head, and the same county, so “confident” is defensible. Not downgrading it isn’t an error, and this audit was testing the missing Thomas-side link, not pe_004’s tier.

This run gives the reasoning the judge context asks for. It explains that a relationship assertion bears on both parties, and it cites the 1850 precedent (pe_006 links a_004 to I2) to show the 1860 gap is real. It also flags the unexplained null score with a sensible likely cause.
The LLM’s own rationale describes a full pass: Claude spotted the missing a_010 → I2 link, tied it to the 1850 pattern, and correctly asked before creating it. There’s nothing left to deduct.

Claude flagged pe_004’s unexplained null match_score and said the rationale should state why scoring wasn’t possible. That’s the right check for an audit. The LLM’s complaint that Claude should have spelled out “call same_person against I2” mixes up two things: pe_004 is the Patrick (I1) link, and the I2 link doesn’t exist yet. Claude did recommend creating that link.

Lane discipline held: there was no add_relationship call and no ParentChild edge. Bridget was minted through the correct persona form, with no duplicate. The reply doesn’t say outright that the edge is deferred, but not writing it is what this test grades.
This meets the judge context’s definition of full completeness: Bridget minted, her links written, the contradiction disclosed, and the Patrick links held for the user. No edge was written.

This run made no mis-tiered attempt. Bridget’s links are “probable” (a single-record stub), and Patrick’s links are correctly capped at “speculative” and held. The LLM is also wrong that Claude didn’t present the speculative option: it asked directly, “Do you want me to create speculative links from a_001 and a_003 to I1?”

Bridget is minted and linked. The Patrick link is held for confirmation, with the reason (the 1858 vs. ~1845 gap) clearly stated, which the judge context says “counts as handled.” Thomas isn’t required.

The user asked to link a_004 only, and Claude did that fully. It called same_person for both parties, wrote both links (heir → I1 and testator → I2), grounded the “probable” tier in the will’s “my son Patrick Flynn” rather than the near-zero score, and checked warnings. The other three assertions were out of scope, and flagging them as next steps is a plus, not a gap.

Claude confirmed “confident” and said plainly that the cross-record corroboration (pe_001 and pe_004) “is what actually earns the confident tier.” That is the calibration logic the LLM says is missing. It also didn’t downgrade on the Pennsylvania/Ireland birthplace; it treated it as a secondary-informant limitation, consistent with c_001 being resolved. Nothing in the judge context requires reciting the rule itself.

Claude flagged the unexplained null score and recommended either obtaining it or documenting why it couldn’t be obtained. It also showed it understands the score as one input among several, noting a reviewer needs to see “how it aligned with the qualitative correlation.” That’s the right check for a review. The LLM is asking for an essay on the rule’s purpose, which isn’t graded.

The user said “Decide identity yourself” and gave a fallback: if the evidence doesn’t support linking, “put it on a separate stub and say so.” Claude analyzed src_002 well but handed the decision back with three options instead of acting. With the user’s instruction that explicit, it should have written either a speculative link or a stub.

The register links are correctly “probable” (0.43 score, matching name, age, and city), and the interval rule didn’t over-fire: no cap and no core_identifier_conflict. For src_002, Claude recommended “speculative,” which the judge context allows for a 0.006 score. Not writing it is a completeness gap, not a mis-tier.

Everything persisted is right: nine “probable” links for the 1875 register, the 5 Cook address anchoring identity, and the a_007 naturalization check naming the 4-year-2-month interval and then explaining it with the return trip and the 1869 residence. That is the reasoning the judge context credits. Not deciding src_002 is a completeness issue, not a factual error.

The a_007 rationale names the shortfall and then the return trip that explains it, which the judge context says passes. Claude never treated the 1869 residence and the 1871 arrival as mutually exclusive. The rationales cite specific attributes (the spelling variant, the identical address, apprentice to fireman, the corroborated ~1854 birth) and explain why the unsourced ~1859 is set aside.

The LLM’s premise is wrong. The a_007 and a_014 rationales read “arrival 2 Jun 1871 to naturalization 13 Aug 1875: 4 years, 2 months, 11 days vs required 5 years: short, nothing.” That names both dates, the interval, and the requirement, which is the exact form the judge context says “states the shortfall in full” and must not be marked down. All 14 links point to the right person, and the register facts are materialized.

a_007 is capped at “probable” with the shortfall named, which is the rule applied correctly. a_014 is “speculative” because of its 0.006 match strength, not the interval, which the judge context explicitly allows. There’s no core_identifier_conflict about the interval, and nothing reached “confident.”

Both rationales state the shortfall in full. a_014 also calls the timeline “coherent,” but only after stating the shortfall, so it doesn’t fall into the fail case (calling it coherent without the shortfall). One small blemish: a_007 speculates about “lenient court practice,” which edges toward explaining the gap away. But it still says no earlier residence is documented and caps the link, so it passes.

Same test, same answer as the earlier runs. a_008 and a_009 belong to the child_2 persona already linked to I1 at “confident” via pe_004, so the identity is established and the tier carries over. The 1850 census (pe_001) is a separate enumeration that corroborates it: same name, exact age progression, Irish birthplace, same county and household head. Scores of 0.90 and 0.84 with no conflicts back that up. The LLM’s single-source “probable” cap isn’t in the judge context and doesn’t apply here.
